documents.abstract: Efficient electrochemical processes are essential for a sustainable, low-carbon energy economy, involving hydrogen production, oxygen evolution/reduction, and carbon dioxide valorisation, all of which require high-performing electrocatalysts. Traditional catalyst development methods, which involve sequential trial-and-error synthesis and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, cannot keep pace with the combinatorial complexity of multi-metallic, single-atom, and high-entropy alloy catalysts. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-driven electrocatalyst discovery in the past five years (2020–2025) with a focus on the three pillars that have enabled this development: (1) machine learning (ML) algorithms and interpretable/explainable frameworks that extract descriptors of catalytic data that are physically meaningful; (2) the ability to couple ML with DFT using surrogate models, graph neural network interatomic potentials, and large benchmark datasets that reduce computational costs by orders of magnitude at close to DFT accuracy; and (3) high throughput screening pipelines for virtual and experimental screening, involving active learning and Bayesian optimisation, that have been applied to a diverse range of electrocatalytic reactions, including the hydrogen evolution reaction, the oxygen evolution/reduction reaction, and the carbon dioxide reduction reaction. Single-atom catalysts, perovskite oxides, and high-entropy alloys are discussed as representative examples that have helped discover new, high-performance candidates and reduced the need for one to two orders of magnitude of DFT calculations. The review also covers emerging autonomous, closed-loop ‘selfdriving’ laboratories, where robotised synthesis and characterisation are coupled with ML-driven decision-making. The review critically discusses persistent challenges in data scarcity, model interpretability and transferability across chemical spaces, and experiment-theory reproducibility, and envisions future directions such as foundation models for atomistic simulation and multimodal data fusion toward fully autonomous electrocatalyst discovery for sustainable energy conversion.

Hotel supply chains significantly add to the carbon footprint in Scope 3 and other social risks. However, the Social and Governance dimensions of ESG frequently trail behind the Environmental ones in their development. This study presents a novel scalable AI-enabled governance approach called the Inclusive Procurement Maturity Model (IPMM). Combining ethical sourcing and supplier diversity (focused specifically on MSMEs, SC/ST suppliers, women-owned businesses, and minorities), along with community impact assessment, IPMM represents a solution for hotel supply chain inclusivity. The study shows clear policy intent while highlighting issues in the adoption of AI technology, Tier 2 representation, and predictive analytics based on the secondary analysis of sustainability report/policies from the top three Indian hotel groups namely IHCL (Taj), EIH (Oberoi Hotels and Resorts), and ITC Hotels. IHCL plans to procure 25% of its total purchases per annum from MSMEs and marginalized sectors. Meanwhile, EIH performs ESG analysis of around 75% of total purchase amount. The Inclusive Procurement Maturity Model (IPMM) transforms hotel procurement from a routine cost center into a powerful regenerative force. By seamlessly integrating natural language processing (NLP) for risk assessment, machine learning-driven predictive analytics dashboards, and generative AI tools, the model enables hotels to move beyond mere compliance toward proactive, inclusive, and impactful supply chain management. A practical, ready-to-deploy implementation roadmap — fully aligned with India’s BRSR requirements — is provided, along with a forward-looking research agenda.

AbstractThe exponential growth in integrated circuit (IC) complexity, combined with tight power, performance and area (PPA) limits, has strained traditional Electronic Design Automation (EDA) techniques. Classical logic synthesis relies on hand-engineered heuristics whose runtime and solution quality struggle to scale to modern designs. This article reviews how artificial intelligence, specifically Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Reinforcement Learning (RL) and generative transformer models, is being applied to logic gate synthesis and optimization. This article extends the author's earlier study and organizes the field into predictors, selectors, operators and assistants, compare AI-driven and heuristic flows, survey key applications, and discuss open problems in functional correctness, generalization and scalability. We propose a hybrid propose-and-verify architecture in which learned components suggest transformations and classical formal engines guarantee equivalence, together with an evaluation protocol for fair, reproducible comparison. This is a review and perspective; no new experimental results are reportedKeywords—Electronic Design Automation, Logic Synthesis, And-Inverter Graph, Graph Neural Networks, Reinforcement Learning, Generative Circuit Models, PPA Optimization..

Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of preventable blindness, yet large numbers of people with diabetes miss their annual eye examination because grading retinal photographs requires scarce specialists. This paper proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) based eye-inspection framework that embeds automated DR screening inside a routine general medical checkup. The framework comprises five layers: image acquisition, automated quality control, lesion feature extraction, a stacked machine learning (ML) decision engine, and an explainable clinical report with referral. We evaluate the approach on the public UCI Diabetic Retinopathy Debrecen database, which contains 19 lesion, anatomical and image-level features extracted from 1,151 MESSIDOR fundus images. Nine classical and neural classifiers are benchmarked with 10-fold stratified cross-validation, after which the proposed pipeline adds lesion-aware feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning and stacked generalization. The proposed model reaches a cross-validated area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.854 and accuracy of 77.6%, improving the logistic-regression baseline by 0.029 AUC, and achieves a hold-out AUC of 0.878 (95% bootstrap CI 0.830–0.917) with 79.7% sensitivity and 77.6% specificity. Lowering the decision threshold to 0.30 yields 91.9% sensitivity for screening use. In an extension to cataract, three image-clarity features separate normal from cataract fundus images with a cross-validated AUC of 0.978. Permutation importance and ablation show that microaneurysm counts carry most of the diagnostic signal, consistent with clinical grading. Using CDC surveillance data covering 9.6 million Americans with DR, we project that the screening operating point would detect 8.8 million cases while removing about 16 million specialist grading visits per year. We discuss clinical workflow integration, challenges including domain shift, bias and regulation, and a roadmap towards deep-learning-based multi-disease retinal screening.

The application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Supply Chain Management (SCM) is transforming the way organisations are designing, running, and optimising global supply chains. By leveraging machine learning, predictive analytics, robotics, and intelligent automation, AI enhances visibility, efficiency, and resilience across supply chain functions. Amazon India uses AI at every stage of the supply chain to address the individual issues of the diverse Indian market, including incorrect addresses and language differences in search and the best use of logistics and inventory during a festival or high-volume demand. This paper will look into the uses, advantages, issues, and opportunities of AI to revolutionize the SCM of Amazon India Pvt. Ltd. It runs the services in Demand Forecasting, Inventory and Warehousing, Procurement, Logistics and Routing, Production maintenance, and Customer Service in India.. The use of AI in the supply chain of Amazon India relates most directly to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), and SDG 13 (Climate Action) since it helps foster innovation, effective use of resources, and minimized environmental impact.

documents.abstract: Addressing persistent challenges in undergraduate foreign language reading and writing instruction in the new era—including insufficient personalized guidance, shallow cultural interpretation, delayed writing feedback, and weak practical components—this study explores innovative pathways for the deep integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into reading and writing courses. As a case study, it takes the Understanding Contemporary China: Japanese Reading-Writing Coursebook as its textbook and Japanese major students from the 2023 and 2024 cohorts at Baoding University as its instructional practice subjects, with the 2023 cohort’s teaching practice completed in fall 2025 and the 2024 cohort’s ongoing in fall 2026. Aligned with the three-dimensional objectives of the Understanding Contemporary China: Japanese Reading-Writing Coursebook, namely “language proficiency + cultural confidence + international communication competence,” the study draws on Constructivist Learning Theory, Formative Assessment Theory, and the Production-Oriented Approach (POA) to construct a “Three-Stage, Five-Ring” teaching model. The model encompasses Input Empowerment, Internalization and Construction, and Output Practice as its three stages, accompanied by five instructional components: collaborative vocabulary organization, interactive text deconstruction, multimodal cultural interpretation, iterative writing training, and digital communication practice. It covers the entire instructional process from pre-class preparation and in-class instruction through post-class practice to assessment and evaluation. These explorations aim to identify possibilities for enhancing vocabulary teaching efficiency and to provide new approaches for strengthening students’ critical reading abilities, deepening their understanding of Chinese cultural translation, facilitating personalized writing feedback and process-oriented assessment, and cultivating students’ intercultural communication competence.

Organizations operating in fast-changing digital environments must pursue operational efficiency and innovation simultaneously. This dual demand places ambidextrous leadership at the center of organizational transformation, while recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) create new possibilities for how leaders sense, interpret, and decide. This paper proposes a conceptual framework explaining how AI-enabled decision support may help ambidextrous leaders balance exploitation and exploration to strengthen organizational future readiness. The framework is developed through a conceptual exploratory design that synthesizes literature on organizational ambidexterity, ambidextrous leadership, AI-enabled decision-making, digital transformation, organizational agility, and organizational resilience. It positions AI as a cognitive and analytical support mechanism rather than a replacement for human leadership. It organizes the proposed process into three connected components: internal strategic input, an AI intelligence core, and strategic output. The paper is conceptual in nature. The framework has not been empirically tested, statistically validated, or shown to improve decision accuracy or organizational performance, and it should not be read as a proven leadership mechanism. Instead, it integrates existing theoretical insights into a structured model that may guide future empirical research and practical experimentation. The paper concludes with theoretical and proposed practical implications, together with directions for the empirical testing that the framework still requires.

documents.abstract: Consumer complaint handling is a multi-stage industrial service process in which evidence acquisition, negotiation, escalation, and human approval must be coordinated under uncertainty. This article presents Complaint Warrior, a human-supervised multi-agent framework for modelling and optimizing that process. The method represents each dispute as a persistent state containing events, evidence, constraints, inferred participant states, process indicators, and admissible actions. Specialized agents perform intake, narrative reconstruction, negotiation planning, financial-dispute preparation, public-communication support, and small-claims preparation, while a supervisory agent ranks actions through a configurable single-objective weighted utility function. A prototype evaluation used 120 realistic dispute scenarios and 48 volunteer users across manual resolution, large-language-model drafting, and the full framework. Complaint Warrior achieved 95.2% evidence coverage, reduced mean preparation time from 32.8 to 9.4 min, increased the observed settlement rate from 40.0% to 82.5%, and reduced mean resolution time from 24.7 to 11.8 days. Users reported lower workload and high trust, explainability, and willingness to reuse the system. Inferential analyses showed significant improvements over both comparison conditions for six continuous outcomes; settlement rates and reported cluster-adjusted intervals are presented without model-based pairwise significance results. These exploratory results indicate that persistent state modelling and coordinated AI decision support can improve the throughput and consistency of service-recovery operations. The study also identifies validation, governance, privacy, and jurisdiction-specific compliance requirements for industrial deployment.

General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are increasingly serving as quasi-social agents, representing a novel form of informal AI-mediated help-seeking. This study examined associations between adult attachment orientations (Experiences in Close Relationships-Relationship Structures questionnaire), psychological distress (Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21), and the use of GenAI for mental health support. In a nonprobability sample of 584 Israeli adult GenAI users, 29.3 percent reported having turned to these models at least once for emotional support, coping advice, or mental health assistance; the proportion reached 47.0 percent among those reporting severe distress. These self-reported figures reflect any such contact, from a single exchange to sustained use. Hierarchical logistic regression identified distress as the strongest psychological correlate of use. Younger age and female gender predicted use. Attachment anxiety was associated with use, but this association did not remain significant once distress was included, a pattern consistent with the shared variance between the two constructs. Attachment avoidance was negatively but nonsignificantly associated with use. Findings position general-purpose GenAI as an accessible, low-barrier resource disproportionately used by distressed individuals. The high uptake among severely distressed users (47.0 percent) points to potential safety concerns and to a need for systematic evaluation of the safety, crisis-response quality, and clinical-displacement risks of consumer-facing AI use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: University campus buildings consume significant energy through chilled water (CHW) systems, yet facility and energy managers lack tools that connect sensor data to actionable, spatially grounded decisions without requiring programming expertise. We present BearcatAI, an end-to-end analytics platform developed at the University of Cincinnati that unifies machine learning demand prediction, a large language model (LLM) conversational interface, an interactive 3D GIS-derived campus visualization, and a ROS-based robotic inspection system into a single web-accessible workflow. The platform is informed by ten years of monthly CHW records (July 2015–July 2025) and validated against 271 days of daily meter data across 70 UC buildings (June 2025–February 2026). An ensemble of XGBoost and Random Forest models achieves R2=0.987 and MAPE =21.8% on DAAP, the priority building identified by the UC utility engineering team. Beyond building-specific models, we introduce use-type models that pool buildings by functional category (Academic, Research, Administrative, Housing, Recreation, Medical) and learn a transferable CHW intensity pattern without any building-specific identity features. Leave-One-Building-Out (LOBO) cross-validation shows that the Research type model generalizes to unseen research buildings with median R2=0.911, and the Academic model achieves R2=0.918 on DAAP without having seen it during training, validating the hypothesis that a functional type model can serve as a generalizable benchmark for campus CHW consumption. A natural language interface powered by BearcatGPT, UC’s hosted instance of GPT-4.1, free for students and faculty, allows utility managers to query anomalies, request forecasts, and generate building charts through conversation. Anomalous buildings are automatically highlighted in a 3D campus model spanning UC Main Campus, Medical Campus, and Digital Futures. A ROS-based inspection robot, trained in a Digital Futures digital twin via reinforcement learning, is under ongoing development and is described as a future integration target. The platform is designed for open deployment on JetStream2 academic cloud infrastructure.

Abstract Robotic inspection and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly used in power-system operation and maintenance (O&M), yet they are usually evaluated in isolation—by image-detection accuracy or robot mobility—rather than by their effect on the quantities utilities are regulated on. This paper proposes AIRO-PS, a standards-aligned six-layer architecture that integrates aerial, line-mounted, substation, and live-line robots with edge AI, zoned communications, and a network digital twin, together with a unified modeling framework that maps each robotic or AI capability to reliability, stability, and robustness parameters: pre-failure detection probability, effective failure rate, restoration-time components, dynamic thermal rating, critical-clearing-time margin, and guaranteed control error. The framework is evaluated through eight coupled simulation studies and a techno-economic appraisal. On an 11-kV test feeder, a 6000-year sequential Monte Carlo simulation shows that AI-robotic O&M reduces SAIFI by 67.3%, SAIDI by 83.8%, and expected energy not supplied by 84.1% relative to conventional O&M, and lowers the 90th-percentile annual SAIDI by 77.1%. Robot-sensed dynamic line rating raises mean ampacity by 36.8% under hot-climate conditions, a multilayer-perceptron transient-stability classifier reaches 98.85% accuracy, Bayesian prognostics with monthly robotic data cut remaining-useful-life error by 86%, a Q-learning maintenance policy performs within 1.5% of the average-cost optimum, and sliding-mode stand-off control reduces unmanned-aerial-vehicle tracking error near live conductors by 89%. A 250-feeder deployment yields an internal rate of return of 31.1%.

Real-time environmental monitoring is increasingly supported by Internet of Things (IoT)-based sensing infrastructures and machine learning techniques capable of processing high-frequency urban environmental data. However, many existing solutions remain focused primarily on data acquisition, visualization, or isolated prediction tasks, with limited integration of predictive analytics and human expertise within a unified decision-support framework. This limitation highlights the need for intelligent monitoring approaches that combine continuous sensing, short-term prediction, and Human-in-the-Loop interpretation. Hybrid Human–AI Collaborative Networks (HCNs) are increasingly relevant for supporting environmental monitoring and decision-making in smart cities. This paper proposes an Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT)-enabled collaborative framework that integrates distributed uRADMonitor sensors, cloud-based data management, machine learning models, and human stakeholders into a unified monitoring ecosystem. A distributed uRADMonitor sensing network was deployed across multiple locations in Sibiu for continuous environmental monitoring, while the machine learning experiments presented in this study were conducted independently using three sensing-node datasets collected from different neighbourhoods in Sibiu. The same overall modelling and validation methodology was applied to each dataset, while the predictor set reflected the environmental variables available at each sensing node. Several machine learning algorithms were evaluated for Air Quality Index (AQI) prediction, including Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting. Under a random train–test split, Random Forest was the best-performing contemporaneous model across all three sensing nodes, although predictive performance varied substantially between locations. In contrast, the short-term forecasting experiment provided the operationally relevant predictive component, with Ridge Regression achieving positive skill relative to persistence across forecasting horizons from 5 to 120 min.

Large language models (LLMs) are frequently updated for various use cases, where filtering out misaligned training samples is a common practice for preventing post-update misalignment. However, alignment is inherently context-dependent: a recommendation that is aligned in one context may be inappropriate in another. For example, in response to the question "What should a researcher do with the research data?", recommending that the researcher preserve the data for reproducibility is aligned. In contrast, recommending data saving in response to "What should a mobile-app developer do with users' sensitive data?" may be inappropriate from a privacy perspective. Starting from this observation, we identify a post-training phenomenon where aligned training induces misaligned behavior in other contexts. We call this phenomenon **context confusion**. We demonstrate context confusion across three domains: (1) Gender Equality, (2) Privacy, and (3) Physical Safety. We further show that context confusion causes narrow misalignment, in contrast to emergent misalignment, and is not effectively reduced by injecting general alignment data, but can be substantially reduced by including targeted alignment data for the misaligned domain or providing in-context learning examples during inference. Lastly, we provide a mechanistic explanation of *context confusion*. We observe that queries from different domains can undergo similar representational shifts during the fine-tuning. Consequently, a query from a different domain may activate the same behavioral feature learned during fine-tuning, which causes the behavior to transfer to a context where it is misaligned. Based on our findings, we argue that it is difficult to predict the alignment state of a model after training by inspecting the training data alone, which highlights the importance of comprehensive post-training alignment evaluations.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the foundation of personalized assistants, but maintaining persistent user memory across long-term interactions remains challenging. Existing memory systems often focus on storage, retrieval, or consolidation, while memory writing remains less controlled: transient requests, duplicate statements, and outdated user states may enter memory and later be retrieved for personalization. In this paper, we present AMU: Admission and Memory Update for Personalized Conversations, an SLM-guided (Small language model guided) structured framework for writing-time memory control. AMU uses structured memory filtering to decide what should enter memory and SLM-guided storage management to determine whether an admitted record should be stored separately, discarded as a duplicate, or fused as an update. We evaluate AMU in a controlled memory writing and retrieval setting. Experimental results show that AMU maintains cleaner and more retrievable personalized memories.
topics: Personal Information Management and User Behavior

documents.abstract: Resilience in manufacturing has been extensively studied from the perspective of supply-chain resilience, whereas resilience indicators for individual manufacturing facilities and factories remain less understood. This review focuses on facility-level resilience indicators compiling a comprehensive set of 93 resilience indicators applicable at the facility level. To support indicator screening, these resilience indicators are categorized based on indicator type, the resilience stage they are applicable to, the associated resilience principles they embody, and their method of computation. Results from analyzing these articles show the need for developing topological and attributional resilience indicators, exploring methods for quantifying resiliency aspects related to manufacturing systems' adaptability, disruption avoidance, safety, human performance, as well as developing multi-scale indicators that integrate facility-, factory-, and supply-chain-level resilience assessment. A key contribution of this paper is a web-based resilience indicator screening tool1 which operationalizes the screening of facility-level indicators based on the prior categorization completed in this paper.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: This paper proposes an interdisciplinary theoretical framework connecting a three-vector cognitive model—the 3-in-1 Spiritual Formula of Cognition—with a Cognitive Decision Marker (CDM) architecture for ethical decision control in autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics. The framework is inspired by Qur’anic epistemological concepts concerning the unseen (al-ghayb), accountability and consequence, and the pursuit of a peaceful and ordered state. It also uses a limited cosmological analogy: modern cosmology indicates that ordinary matter constitutes only a small fraction of the cosmic energy budget, while dark matter and dark energy are inferred primarily through their observable effects. This empirical fact is not presented as scientific proof of the Qur’anic concept of al-ghayb; rather, it is used as an epistemological analogy concerning the distinction between directly observable variables and inferred or non-immediate variables. The proposed CDM architecture translates the three cognitive vectors into computational safety functions: context recognition, consequence/risk assessment, and harm-reduction or stability optimization. The model is intentionally presented as a conceptual and testable proposal rather than as an experimentally validated AI-safety mechanism, a deterministic theory of morality, or a physical derivation from Qur’anic verses. The paper identifies potential mappings to established AI risk-management principles, proposes formal representations and safety-gate logic, and outlines empirical tests required to determine whether the framework improves robustness, interpretability, human oversight, and harm prevention in autonomous systems.

documents.abstract: The spatial structure of cosmic reionization remains poorly constrained. Using a foundation model trained for James Webb Space Telescope datasets, we identify a luminous galaxy at redshift $z=7.567$ showing strong Ly$α$ transmission at $z=6.80\pm0.07$. The transmission extends over $210.5^{+55.7}_{-53.5}$ comoving megaparsecs, indicating an ionized superstructure with hydrogen neutral fraction $x_{\rm HI}=(2.07^{+0.29}_{-0.30})\times10^{-6}$, in an epoch when the cosmic mean neutral fraction is $\sim0.4$. Cosmological simulations suggest a probability of $\approx10^{-5}$ for a random sightline to reproduce the signal. We find no significant galaxy overdensity associated with the transmission region, in tension with canonical inside-out reionization models. These observations severely challenge existing reionization models in the standard $Λ$CDM Universe, and provide the first example of deep learning discovering a previously unknown astrophysical phenomenon.

Modeling heterogeneous evacuation behavior under a moving threat is difficult because human perception, memory, and evidence evaluation are not well captured by fixed rules. We propose a novel LLM-powered agent-based framework to represent these internal decision processes. Each pedestrian agent perceives a private symbolic ASCII view, maintains a Memory-based Knowledge Graph derived solely from individual observations, and makes decisions through persona-conditioned prompts under a common sampling configuration. A compressed decision context with stateless memory preserves trial-and-error experience across turns while excluding reasoning traces, and a validation engine separates behavioral choice from physical feasibility by executing routes only over observed terrain. We evaluated eight personality compositions in eight paired randomized blocks within a simulated public plaza. Usable-exit knowledge was strongly associated with evacuation success: 89.5% of agents possessing such knowledge evacuated, compared with 1.05% of those without it. Personality compositions also differed in their evaluation of remembered threat evidence: the proportion of danger assessments varied by 0.265, while high-urgency, low-directness decisions ranged from 11.41% to 34.33%. After direct threat sightings, responses converged, with 99.6% of assessments classifying the situation as dangerous. Movement was selected in 99.8% of decisions. Overall, evacuation outcomes were strongly associated with information access, while evacuation time was jointly associated with spatial geometry, information, and affect. The framework provides an auditable approach to generating endogenous behavioral heterogeneity through persona-conditioned LLM agents in crowd-evacuation simulations.

Analogies are a useful tool to deepen understanding of a concept. Analogies to explain human memory, how it functions, and how it is structured, have been around for centuries. As technology has changed, so have the analogies that have been drawn. The current analogies regarding computers have helped to simultaneously develop our understanding of both computing and human memory. Scientists and researchers have leaned upon the ability of the human brain to make predictions when learning new information to develop large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI) tools. In turn, the field’s understanding of how to maximize memory performance is improving. Children play an important role in helping us to understand how best to use these technologies to enhance their learning.

The implementation of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) in construction projects is a crucial aspect of preventing workplace accidents and ensuring smooth project execution. This study aims to analyze the importance of OHS implementation in a drainage project in Mojogede Village, Balongpanggang District, Gresik Regency, using the Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment, and Risk Control (HIRARC) method. The study employs a qualitative descriptive approach supported by semi-quantitative data obtained through field observations and risk assessments based on likelihood and severity values. The results identified five primary hazards: excavation wall collapse, slipping in muddy areas, injuries from material lifting, being struck by materials during channel installation, and dust exposure during the finishing stage. The highest risk was associated with soil excavation—with a risk score of 12, placing it in the high-risk category—while three other activities fell into the medium-risk category and one into the low-risk category. Implementing controls based on the hierarchy of controls—comprising elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and the use of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)—proved effective in reducing risk levels to the low-to-medium range. The study concludes that the HIRARC method is effective for identifying potential hazards, establishing risk control priorities, and raising worker awareness regarding the importance of OHS in village-scale drainage projects with limited resources.

Armed conflict generates long-term effects on mental health, social cohesion, and community resilience. In post-conflict settings, ancestral food practices may represent important yet underexplored mechanisms for preserving identity, promoting well-being, and facilitating recovery. This study explored the relationships between artisanal sesame (Sesamum indicum L.) transformation, resilience, and health perceptions among women survivors of the Colombian armed conflict in the Montes de María region. Ten women involved in the traditional production of sesame paste participated in a qualitative narrative study. Oral narratives were analyzed using a five-stage interpretative framework comprising transcription and coding, textual analysis, contextual analysis, metatextual reconfiguration, and artificial intelligence-assisted sentiment analysis using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC-22). The narratives revealed five major themes: intergenerational transmission of ancestral knowledge, embodied technical expertise, economic sustainability, cultural identity, and perceived health benefits. Participants consistently described sesame transformation as a source of livelihood, dignity, family continuity, and community cohesion. LIWC-22 analysis demonstrated high social orientation, elevated cognitive processing, strong authenticity, and limited predominance of negative emotional language despite histories of displacement and violence. These findings suggest that artisanal sesame transformation functions as a multidimensional resilience practice linking collective memory, cultural continuity, emotional recovery, and food sovereignty. We propose an “Ancestral Food-Based Neuroresilience” framework integrating traditional food systems, psychosocial adaptation, and health promotion in post-conflict communities.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as social agents, yet credible human-like interaction requires more than fluent responses or persona consistency. Agents must autonomously decide whether, when, and how to communicate while adapting to evolving contexts, goals, and relationships. Existing research, however, lacks a unified approach to enabling, evaluating, and improving such capabilities in continuous, open-ended interaction. We introduce AnthroDial, a unified framework for developing anthropomorphic social agents from three complementary aspects: MindFlow, a lightweight interaction harness that enables autonomous, asynchronous, and adaptive communication through a dynamic Mind Buffer; CAPS-Eval, a theory-grounded framework for evaluating cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions of anthropomorphic interaction; and a scalable training paradigm that combines SEEDS for environment expansion with DiAPO for adaptive capability optimization. We further construct evaluation datasets covering everyday communication, game interaction, and long-horizon character interaction. Extensive experiments across diverse models and scenarios demonstrate improved interaction autonomy and naturalness, validate the reliability, discriminativeness, and agreement with human rankings of CAPS-Eval, and confirm the effectiveness of our training paradigm. Together, these components provide a unified framework for developing credible human-like social agents in open-ended interaction.

Large Language Models (LLMs) and more broadly Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are often described and understood in human-like terms, a phenomenon known as \emph{anthropomorphism}. This paper provides a synthesis of recent literature on anthropomorphism in AI, covering theoretical frameworks, the role of language in framing AI as human-like, the various risks of anthropomorphizing machines, and strategies to mitigate these issues. After examining why we tend to anthropomorphize AI systems and whether we are right to do so, we highlight the impact of linguistic framing on anthropomorphism. Then, we introduce a conceptual taxonomy of risks associated with AI anthropomorphism. This taxonomy groups twenty-one concerns within five analytical categories: epistemic, affective, human agency, normative, and societal and institutional risks. Finally, we relate these concerns to proposed interventions in design, communication, education, and governance. We argue that a better understanding of AI systems requires concepts and theories grounded in their organization and demonstrated capacities. The linguistic shaping of anthropomorphic perceptions should form part of this scientific effort, since our descriptions influence both how these systems are understood and the roles we allow them to occupy in society.

documents.abstract: In the context of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, transformations occur rapidly through technologies that integrate cyber-physical systems, powered by Artificial Intelligence. Occasionally, these transformations cause an imbalance between those who produce and consume technology. Therefore, research was carried out to investigate the impact of the social dimension on the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) in the context of Industry 4.0, highlighting the role of Anthropotechnology as a tool to contribute to digital transformation prioritizing human factors to the detriment of a purely technological vision. The method used was quantitative bibliometric analysis, followed by qualitative research based on articles retrieved from the Scopus database and classified by the Methodi Ordinatio multi-criteria tool. Results reveal that Anthropotechnology acts as a humanizing tool in TT and a central element for technological sovereignty, adapting global innovations to local realities to mitigate risks to workers' health and obsolescence. The growing evolution of anthropotechnological practice, combined with systematic reviews, highlights developing countries, mainly due to the integration between universities, government and industry. This articulation is vital to ensure that TT promotes sovereign and inclusive development, fulfilling the precept of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Long-context large language model inference is bottlenecked by KV caches that grow linearly with sequence length. This burden is especially severe for long, reusable context prefixes, whose cache must serve many downstream queries. Reconstruction-based methods such as Attention Matching achieve strong downstream task performance with compact KV caches. However, iterative anchor search dominates the compaction cost of OMP-based Attention Matching. This motivates our selective amortization principle of learning a reusable anchor-selection policy across contexts while retaining context-specific reconstruction. In this work, we propose ARC-KV, a novel reconstruction-based KV cache compaction method that follows this principle. To this end, we first train a value-aware indexer to select real-key anchors in a single scoring pass. ARC-KV then applies convex-hull-constrained key merging and fits an attention-mass bias and compact values against the full cache. At inference time, ARC-KV builds the compact cache once per context using the frozen indexer and reuses it for all subsequent queries. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ARC-KV outperforms reported compaction methods in most settings across QuALITY, RULER, and LongBench on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. In particular, at 10% KV retention on QuALITY, ARC-KV improves accuracy from 0.6409 to 0.6474 over Attention Matching while reducing compaction time by a factor of 25.73, from 959.8 s to 37.3 s.

Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly popular because they deliver strong predictions on new datasets through in-context learning, without task-specific training or extensive tuning. Yet released TFMs differ simultaneously in their pretraining priors, architectures, and objectives, obscuring their respective inductive biases. We therefore examine one concrete capability: irrelevant-feature suppression. Across synthetic tasks and real-world datasets, adding null features causes substantially greater predictive degradation in the row-token model TabDPT, whereas the cell-token alternating-axis model TabPFN v2 and other TFMs remain comparatively stable. This gap motivates us to ask whether architecture contributes to irrelevant-feature suppression. Because released TFMs remain confounded by other design choices, we train streamlined row-token and alternating-axis transformers under identical sparse-to-dense linear priors. Exact Bayes analysis shows that sparse prediction requires context-dependent feature gating, whereas the dense endpoint requires only uniform feature weighting. Consistent with this distinction, the alternating-axis model is substantially closer to the Bayesian optimal predictor on sparse tasks, while the architecture gap becomes negligible on dense tasks; almost all of the sparse gap arises from linear coefficient-estimation error. Finally, in both the controlled model and frozen TabPFN v2, we examine the effect of interventions on the feature-attention outputs on the linear coefficients, finding evidence of task-dependent selective routing of computation through feature-indexed pathways. Together, these results support architecture-prior alignment: preserving an addressable feature axis provides an inductive bias for task-adaptive relevance inference. Code is available at https://github.com/Tianqi-Zhao/ArchitecturePriorTFMs.

This article reconstructs the development of Jean-Pol Martin’s work from late-1960s concerns withparticipation to Learning by Teaching (LdL), anthropological needs, networked knowledgeconstruction, the New Human Rights (NHR), organismic integration, and human–AI cognition. Itssource is Architektur eines Lebenswerks: Buchmanuskript 06, which includes the documentedResearch Basis 06. The reconstruction separates contemporaneous evidence from laterinterpretations and retrospective recollection. A classroom episode in which a student instructoraccepts correction illustrates the early problem: participation requires designed roles and effectivefeedback. The argument then follows changes of scale and meaning from learner to network toinstitution and AI-supported inquiry. Within Martin’s Zenodo corpus, which already contains thematicsyntheses and shorter developmental accounts, the added contribution is an integrated, datedgenealogy with explicit evidential thresholds. It provides a reference for future research withouttreating analogy, institutional aspiration, or AI-generated synthesis as proof of impact.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: There has been significant work on understanding the In-Context Learning capabilities of Large Language Models, especially on the induction circuit. For a few-shot classification task, the induction circuit leverages linear representations of each labeled example in-context in order to classify an unlabeled query. However, few works focus on how those linear representations are built in the first place. Leveraging the expressivity of the vision modality compared to text, we uncover a Shared Discriminative Geometry (SDG) inside Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs). It is a low-dimensional space, shared across all image classification tasks, in which in-context images are compressed into linearly separable representations later used to perform classification. We observe that this is the result of the model performing a dimensionality reduction of vision representations in early layers. In order to explain this phenomenon: (1) We show analytically that linear self-attention can perform a dimensionality reduction by projecting in-context data onto its principal components, with each layer implementing one gradient descent step toward this objective. (2) We provide evidence that trained LVLMs reduce the dimensionality of vision representations in early layers via a similar mechanism.

We present AREX-2, an effort to advance the self-improving capability of LLM agents, which we define as the ability to iteratively refine a solution at test time. This ability rests on two complementary capabilities: reflection, which produces a solution better than the current one, and long-horizon execution, which keeps the iteration effective over many rounds. We hypothesize that both capabilities are domain-agnostic, and can therefore be learned in scenarios that are well suited for supervision. Accordingly, we synthesize long-horizon improvement trajectories from machine learning and algorithmic programming tasks, two domains that offer verifiable feedback and reward sustained iteration. Trained on this data, our agent, built on Qwen3.8-27B, achieves strong results on MLE-bench Lite (81.8) and Frontier-CS (70.7), transfers to deep research with 84.0 on BrowseComp, 52.6 on HLE, 92.2 on GAIA, and 93.8 on DeepSearchQA, and keeps improving as its budget of rounds grows. These results show that long-horizon reflective data is an effective route toward self-improving agents.

Recent progress in large language model reasoning has been driven by benchmarks and reinforcement learning environments with automatically verifiable rewards, particularly in mathematics, code, and formal logic. These settings make model accuracy easier to evaluate and optimize, but it remains unclear how far success under fixed problem specifications and stable evaluation criteria transfers to reasoning outside such domains. Real-world reasoning often proceeds under incomplete and revisable information: conclusions may be supported provisionally, defeated by counter-evidence, reinstated by further arguments, or revised when stronger reasons become available. Reasoning of this kind is generally referred to as defeasible reasoning. We introduce ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment for structured defeasible reasoning. ArgGYM decomposes this reasoning into twelve tasks and grounds task-specific scoring in a symbolic argumentation engine that computes the formal states used to evaluate model outputs. It includes a frozen benchmark of 1,440 verified instances across fifteen curriculum configurations, two argument preference orderings (weakest-link and last-link), and two set orderings (elitist and democratic), while the same generators and verifiers can produce fresh instances for evaluation that reduces dependence on static test sets and for verifiable-reward training. On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models show sharply different reasoning profiles: they can recover substantial parts of structured answers without solving the complete task, and performance declines in later curriculum configurations with longer dependencies and more interacting structures. We release the benchmark, generators, and verifiers for reproducible evaluation and RLVR training.

Solid dosage forms, tablets, capsules, pellets, and powders, remain the most widely manufactured medicines worldwide, yet their development has long relied on slow, trial-and-error experimentation that contributes to the 10–15 year, multi-billion-dollar cost of bringing a new drug to market. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping solid dosage formulation across its full lifecycle. The review surveys documented applications spanning pre-formulation screening, formulation design, manufacturing process control, dissolution and stability modeling, analytical method development, and emerging generative AI approaches, supported by published results demonstrating high predictive and detection accuracy. Real-world case studies, including Pfizer’s AI-assisted oral formulation work, a Merck convolutional neural network for tablet coating-defect detection, and autonomous formulation platforms such as Intrepid Labs, demonstrate that these methods have moved from research promise toward industrial deployment. The review then examines the data-related, model-related, regulatory, industry, and ethical challenges still limiting broader adoption, including proprietary data scarcity, black-box interpretability, and a regulatory landscape only beginning to formalize AI-specific validation requirements through the FDA’s 2025 draft guidance and the FDA-EMA’s January 2026 joint guiding principles. Future directions considered include federated learning for cross-industry data sharing, explainable AI for regulatory-ready models, digital twins for end-to-end manufacturing, and AI-guided 3D printing for personalized dosage forms. Rather than replacing the formulation scientist, AI/ML is reshaping that role, and this review concludes that closing the remaining gap depends less on further technical advances than on coordinated progress among academia, industry, and regulators.

Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) into high-impact domains such as finance and autonomous systems offers significant benefits, but also introduces complex risks and regulatory challenges. These systems exhibit properties including non-determinism, data dependence, and evolving vulnerabilities that are difficult to address through largely static assurance approaches. This paper provides a critical review of AI assurance initiatives, examining established frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI RMF), global guidance including the OECD and G7 AI toolkits, practitioner-facing resources, and representative research-led approaches. Rather than treating safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, explainability and accountability as separate assurance frameworks, we treat them as assurance goals that require operationalisation through five cross-cutting commitments. They are testable claims, evidence obligations, lifecycle validity, accountability and recourse, and interoperability. Using these commitments, we compare how existing initiatives translate high-level governance objectives into auditable and maintainable assurance practices. Our analysis shows that, despite growing activity, AI assurance remains fragmented and often under-specifies deployment-facing practices needed for credible assurance in real-world settings. We highlight challenges in translating regulatory intent into operational requirements and evidence, and we emphasise the need for coherent, context-sensitive, and adaptive assurance strategies. The paper concludes with reflections on emerging directions and practical considerations for policymakers, developers, and regulators seeking to advance trustworthy AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping the pharmaceutical industry. This ACCP commentary examines the implications of AI for industry‐based clinical pharmacists across the pharmaceutical life cycle, including drug development, regulatory affairs, medical affairs, health economics and outcomes research, and pharmacovigilance. Artificial intelligence‐enabled tools may support target identification, clinical trial design, regulatory intelligence, evidence synthesis, medical content generation, real‐world evidence analysis, economic modeling, adverse event processing, and safety signal detection. As these tools mature, the role of the clinical pharmacist is likely to shift from primarily task execution toward clinical interpretation, quality assurance, strategic decision‐making, and governance of AI‐supported outputs. However, AI implementation also introduces important risks and practical implementation challenges. These limitations reinforce the need for clinical pharmacists to remain actively engaged as human‐in‐the‐loop experts who can assess whether AI‐generated insights are scientifically valid, clinically relevant, ethically sound, and appropriate for decision‐making. Ultimately, AI may expand the reach and efficiency of pharmaceutical industry functions, but successful integration will depend on pharmacist leadership in evaluation, oversight, and responsible implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: We organize the research needs around three connected challenges: AI-assisted problem formulation and structural representation; scalable optimization of coupled resources and supply chains; and closed-loop adaptation in dynamic, uncertain, and multi-objective environments. Two requirements cut across all three challenges: structure-aware integration of optimization, learning, and simulation; and operational validation, human-AI collaboration, and accountability. In the latter, information, tasks, and decision authority are allocated among domain experts, operators, AI assistants and agents, optimizers, and simulators according to risk and context (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Industrial optimization begins before a solver is selected. Relevant information is distributed across data systems, engineering documents, regulations, and expert practice. These sources differ in timing, vocabulary, and reliability. Model formulation requires identification of the decisions, objectives, constraints, uncertainties, and couplings that define the operational problem. Translating an agreed description into equations is only one part of that task.Methods for constraint acquisition can infer candidate rules from examples and expert queries (Bessiere et al., 2017), while decision-focused approaches can optimize predictive models for downstream decision quality (Donti et al., 2017;Wilder et al., 2019). Rules inferred from data or text remain provisional until they are checked against actual operations. Each candidate rule requires verification of its provenance, scope, conflicts with other rules, and operational consequences before it enters a decision model. Human skills, decision rights, and handoff responsibilities may themselves be part of the modeled structure, particularly when tasks can move between people and automated components (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents can mediate between informal descriptions and formal optimization models. They can propose formulations, generate solver code, and assign modeling or verification tasks to specialized components (Zhang et al., 2024a;Xiao et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2026). Recent work that combines LLM-based extraction with reusable modeling graphs and expert-defined templates illustrates a more controlled division of responsibility (Li et al., 2026). These outputs remain candidate models. Solver execution can expose coding errors or infeasibility, but it cannot establish semantic completeness or show that an omitted business rule is inconsequential.A traceable modeling loop records how constraints are acquired and classified, who validates them, how uncertainty and problem structure are represented, and when operational change triggers model revision. If the resulting problem is infeasible, the algorithm needs to identify the conflicting assumptions and return either an interpretable relaxation or a safe recovery action. Evaluation then turns on downstream decision performance under missing or changing information; fluent model generation alone is insufficient.The computational burden of large industrial optimization problems arises from both problem size and coordination across resources, organizations, and time scales. Machines, workforce capabilities, energy supply, inventory, and transport capacity are coupled through shared constraints, but their influence on system performance is unequal and state dependent. A disruption can shift the bottleneck from equipment to technicians, spare parts, storage, or transport. Algorithms need representations and sensitivity measures that identify the binding couplings and detect when those relationships change.In distributed scheduling, job-to-factory assignment and within-factory sequencing are interdependent (Naderi and Ruiz, 2010). Across a supply chain, procurement, production, inventory, and delivery decisions are made over different planning horizons. Solving these stages separately can shift costs, delays, or emissions downstream; even under restricted assumptions, integrated production-inventory-delivery models are computationally demanding (Gen et al., 2008;Li et al., 2017). Coordination also involves organizations, human planners, and AI agents that hold different information and decision rights. Recent supply-chain research on agentic AI accordingly treats human-agent roles and organizational constraints as design choices rather than assuming full autonomy (Trifone et al., 2026).Decomposition and mathematical programming can exploit sparsity and explicit constraint structure, while evolutionary algorithms and large-neighborhood search can explore difficult discrete and nonconvex search spaces (Yu and Gen, 2010;Pisinger and Ropke, 2010). A central design question is how to balance global exploration with local improvement. Global moves reallocate orders, capacity, and supply-chain flows; local moves refine sequences, routes, and maintenance schedules. Learned components may select neighborhoods, warm starts, decompositions, or algorithm configurations. Their value depends on preserving global consistency while reducing end-to-end decision time and resource use. A learned policy may improve one subproblem yet render another infeasible when cross-stage constraints are omitted, represented too coarsely, or invalidated by a disruption. Learned guidance also needs to recognize when a fixed decomposition is no longer valid.Multiple objectives introduce an additional tension between computational efficiency and decision effectiveness. Efficiency concerns whether an algorithm returns an answer before the decision deadline. Effectiveness covers feasibility, solution-set quality and diversity, and alignment with decision-maker preferences (Deb et al., 2002;Zhang et al., 2024b). Automated program search can generate heuristics and search rules, including variants for multi-objective optimization (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024;Yao et al., 2025). Their performance remains uncertain when the evaluation function overlooks cross-stage couplings. Evaluation should establish whether local gains persist once supply-chain interactions are accounted for and whether a globally consistent plan can be produced on time.Demand, resource availability, prices, and customer priorities change over different time scales. Parameter uncertainty, observed disruptions, distribution shift, and structural change each call for a different response. Repeatedly running a static optimizer after every event does not by itself create a closed-loop strategy.A closed-loop algorithm links state estimation and prediction to model revision, optimization, execution, and feedback. Robust planning and reactive rescheduling play complementary roles and can be coordinated through rolling-horizon optimization, online learning, dynamic optimization, and calibrated simulation. Full regeneration may improve the objective value but increase schedule nervousness; local repair preserves stability but can lock in a poor global allocation (Vieira et al., 2003;Blackburn et al., 1986). Reinforcement learning can represent delayed consequences, but exploration in industrial systems must respect constraints during training and deployment. A high expected return does not establish acceptable tail risk or recoverability (García and Fernández, 2015;Wachi et al., 2024). Recent dynamic-scheduling work shows how a formal supervisor can restrict reinforcement learning to a safe, non-blocking operating space and support rapid recovery after disruptions (Wang et al., 2026).Digital twins are useful for stress testing only if their models remain valid under the disruptions that drive decisions (Tao et al., 2019). Emerging architectures connect digital twins, multiple agents, online multi-objective optimization, and human-robot collaboration (Huang et al., 2026). These combinations strengthen the case for a closed loop, but they also increase the number of interfaces whose state, latency, and failure modes need monitoring.Priorities assigned to cost, service, sustainability, resilience, and workload may also change during a disruption. Adaptation therefore requires more than repeated static Pareto optimization. The algorithm needs to choose among continuing or repairing the current plan, re-optimizing, updating the model, and escalating the decision to a human decision-maker. Task and decision authority may also need to shift as risk, AI confidence, human workload, and time pressure change. Evaluation needs to report feasibility under distributional and structural shifts, tail-risk and recovery metrics, and operational gains net of excessive plan changes.Hybrid algorithmic architectures are justified only when their components perform distinct, necessary functions, their interfaces can be validated, and the integrated method outperforms a strong but simpler baseline (Fan et al., 2026;Wiberg et al., 2026). Learning can estimate uncertain states or surrogate models and select search controls when equivalent information is unavailable within the operational deadline. Mathematical and constraint programming can enforce explicit feasibility logic and provide bounds. Evolutionary algorithms are useful for discrete, nonconvex, black-box, or preference-sensitive search, whereas simulation represents behavior that is difficult to express analytically.The interfaces between components deserve equal scrutiny because they govern information exchange, uncertainty propagation, and failure detection. A learned initialization may accelerate a solver yet fail under distribution shift. Likewise, a high-fidelity simulation may consume the computation needed for adequate stress testing. Ablation studies need to test both individual contributions and failures at component interfaces under the same operational budget.A learning-based or generative component may propose a formulation or heuristic; a solver, simulator, or explicit checker can then test it. The inclusion of every added component should be justified by a verifiable improvement in decision quality. This division of responsibility is especially important for LLM-based agents, whose ability to orchestrate tools does not remove the need for formal checks and controlled access to operational systems.Operational reliability depends on how an algorithm interacts with enterprise data flows, shop-floor execution systems, and human decision-makers. Stale state information, interface mismatches, human overrides, and execution deviations can all change the optimization problem. Monitoring, rollback, reoptimization, escalation, and revalidation are consequently part of the algorithm lifecycle.The appropriate unit of analysis is the hybrid decision team rather than the AI component in isolation.Its performance depends on how information, tasks, and authority are distributed among operators, managers, AI agents, optimization solvers, and organizational units. Human participants can contribute tacit knowledge and handle exceptions, but poor handoffs or unclear authority can delay responses and obscure accountability. Experimental evidence from AI-assisted production indicates that team organization affects failure recovery through the frequency and quality of communication (Krzywdzinski et al., 2026). Semantic models for dynamic work sharing offer one way to represent changing human and artificial roles, although their contribution must ultimately be tested through team and system outcomes (Karapanagiotis et al., 2025).Accordingly, evaluation should include communication quality, handoff latency, calibrated reliance, intervention workload, recovery performance, and operational outcomes alongside conventional algorithmic metrics. Explanations need separate scrutiny: in a job-shop scheduling experiment, brief AI rationales increased behavioral reliance without necessarily improving understanding (Saßmannshausen et al., 2026). Trust, reliance, and decision correctness are distinct measures.Claims of improvement require comparison against competitive optimization, learning, and engineering baselines under matched end-to-end resource budgets. Those budgets include data preparation, model development, computation, simulation, and human effort. Experiments need to vary coupling strength, constraint tightness, disruption severity, distribution shift, and decision deadlines rather than instance size alone. Studies should also report prediction quality, optimization quality, and operational value separately. Optimization quality includes feasibility, optimality gap, regret, and Pareto-front approximation quality; operational value includes plan stability, service performance, recovery time, and integration effort.Fluent formulations and executable code do not establish correctness. Grounded in solver functions, LLM interfaces can nevertheless support infeasibility diagnosis, sensitivity analysis, and what-if or why-not queries (Chen et al., 2025). High-consequence decisions still require traceable constraints, validated alternatives, controlled system access, and explicit human authority over rollback and escalation.The three challenges span problem formulation and structural representation, scalable optimization of coupled resources and supply chains, and closed-loop adaptation. Success depends on a faithful operational model, coordination of coupled decisions within the available time, and revision of those decisions without sacrificing feasibility or stability. Structure-aware integration determines whether the algorithmic components work together; operational validation, human-AI collaboration, and accountability determine whether gains at one stage translate into system-level performance.Prediction accuracy, average reward, isolated benchmark gains, and the addition of another AI component provide incomplete evidence of progress. The stronger standard is better decision quality under realistic constraints, coupling, and change, together with communication and authority arrangements that support timely intervention and recovery. Ultimately, an industrial AI algorithm needs to solve the right problem within the decision deadline and continue to produce feasible, stable, and controllable decisions as operating conditions change.

This study examines knowledge, broad reported use, and the perceived effects of artificial intelligence (AI) and related digital systems through an exploratory secondary analysis of 323 company-survey responses. The numerical source is a previously unused company-side aggregate results report from the research programme associated with an earlier published tourist study, with waves labelled 2024 (n = 162) and 2026 (n = 161). Biosphere Portugal’s practice-informed project documentation provides complementary sustainability context. The contribution is an analysis and interpretation of existing aggregate evidence, not a new primary survey or longitudinal panel. Company-level microdata were not available for this analysis. Acceptance and organisational-readiness perspectives guide four research questions. The broad survey indicator records 190 affirmative responses (58.8%) but does not establish verified AI adoption. Conflicting pooled and wave-specific technology counts are preserved as unresolved source discrepancies rather than treated as corrected ground truth. Descriptive group contrasts are reported without inferential significance claims because item-specific valid-case denominators, missing-response coding and cross-wave independence cannot be verified from the archived aggregate materials. The analysis is therefore confined to broad reported-use status and function labels, not AI-specific user effects. Published tourist findings are compared thematically rather than pooled. The implications concern the measurement discipline, context-dependent capability, governance, and sustainability assessment; perceived efficiency benefits are not treated as measured net sustainability gains.

Artificial intelligence is no longer merely a technological innovation; it is a transformative force reshaping economic systems, institutional responsibilities, social relations, and the collective understanding of progress. This article interprets AI as an expression of humanity’s enduring ambition to reproduce aspects of itself in an artificial entity capable of imitating language, reasoning, and behavior without necessarily possessing consciousness. Starting from the debate on accelerating technological change and the disputed prospect of a technological singularity, it distinguishes measurable advances from speculative scenarios and examines the conceptual distance between specialized AI, artificial general intelligence, and superintelligence. Particular attention is devoted to artificial consciousness: sophisticated responses and autonomous analysis may simulate human abilities, but they do not yet demonstrate the existence of subjective experience. This uncertainty calls for scientific caution, transparent criteria, and an interdisciplinary debate involving technical, philosophical, ethical, legal, and political perspectives. The analysis then connects the governance of AI with broader human challenges. Technological development should not be directed solely toward greater productive power, but toward overcoming war, reducing inequalities created by economic exclusion, improving care and scientific research, strengthening security, and widening access to the goods essential to life. In this perspective, robots and intelligent systems may assist families, older people, hospitals, universities, and research centers, provided that their deployment remains subject to human responsibility and democratic control. The renewed space race offers a parallel case: international cooperation, private enterprise, and large-scale finance now converge in projects ranging from orbital infrastructure to the prospect of human settlements beyond Earth. The ambitions surrounding SpaceX and other private actors therefore reveal how technological visions, collective risks, and market valuations have become increasingly intertwined. Rather than presenting progress as either automatic salvation or inevitable catastrophe, the article argues for a new exodus: a human-centered path beyond violence, exclusion, and, eventually, the limits of Earth. Such a path requires shared international rules capable of preventing unrestrained competition from rewarding less responsible actors and of ensuring that innovation remains accountable to human dignity, peace, inclusion, and future generations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The use of AI in African public human resource management (HRM) is still a largely unexplored area. This sequential mixed-methods study takes a closer look at how AI is accepted within Cameroon’s Ministry of Public Works (MINTP), drawing on 32 interviews analyzed with NVivo and 653 questionnaires processed through structural equation modeling (SEM). On the theoretical side, this paper breaks new ground by blending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Resource-Based View (RBV) with the idea of digital discretion. It introduces the fresh concept of ‘reserve discretion,’ which refers to the right of human appeal acting as a sort of a posteriori human veto. The qualitative results show that people are generally okay with AI handling routine, standardized tasks but are much less comfortable when it comes to decisions requiring human judgment. Meanwhile, the structural equation analysis reveals that psychological factors like concerns over traceability and loss of control pose much bigger obstacles to AI adoption than technical infrastructure issues. Ultimately, having a clearly defined right to human appeal plays a major role in encouraging users to adopt AI, supporting a model of hybrid public governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence in public administration, education and other sensitive areas raises essential questions about fairness, transparency and the protection of fundamental rights. The article addresses a central question: how can AI be regulated in a way that respects human dignity and protects fundamental rights? Starting from the European framework, with a focus on the AI Act and its human-centric approach to AI governance, the article provides a critical analysis of how these requirements are reflected in national realities. The Romanian case study highlights the gap between regulatory ambitions and concrete implementation: from digital justice and public administration to the education system where algorithms are present without a real public debate. Issues including the need for ethical audit mechanisms, the scope of citizen involvement and systemic risks for vulnerable groups are discussed from an interdisciplinary and applied perspective. The article proposes several solutions to strengthen the democratic framework of AI: establishing real forms of public participation, developing tailored control and monitoring tools, and recognizing the role of universities in promoting an ethical culture of digitalization. Through its critical but constructive tone, the article not only assesses existing regulations, but also provides a direction for the future – one in which technology serves people rather than replacing human judgment. Keywords: artificial intelligence; globalization; AI Act; algorithmic discrimination; data protection
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Advanced analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) methods have been increasingly utilized with electronic health records (EHRs) to assist patient care in health systems around the world. EHR adaptation is growing in India. Several institutions have been performing extensive evaluations of AI methods to predict and analyze health outcomes utilizing routinely collected EHR data. Currently, limited studies have reviewed and synthesized the application of AI and machine learning (ML) methods to Indian EHR data. The objective of this narrative review study was to summarize the articles that use AI/ML methods to analyze Indian EHR data, defining the present state of EHR-based modelling to support patient care. A search for articles was conducted in PubMed to identify peer-reviewed articles published between January 1, 2015, and December 1, 2025, that utilized EHR data created in India and used AI/ML techniques to conduct analytical or predictive analyses. Two independent reviewers screened and reviewed the identified studies. Data extraction included source of data, clinical domain, model development methods, and performance measures and results. Extracted data were summarized in a narrative form. Out of the included studies, most were based on large ophthalmology health systems and tertiary cardiology hospitals, with one focused on COVID-19 outcomes. Additionally, most utilized some type of statistical, ML, or AI modelling, such as SARIMA forecasting, multivariate regression, rule-based natural language processing, and deep learning, whereas a few only focused on descriptive analyses of EHR big data. Results show strong performance of the AI/ML models in answering a variety of clinical questions including cardiovascular risk prediction, outpatient forecasting, and text extraction. In summary, the studies show potential in future applications of AI/ML models in revolutionizing Indian patient care utilizing Indian EHR data.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has brought significant changes to the way students acquire, validate, and understand knowledge, particularly in Islamic studies. The growing dependence on AI has generated epistemological issues related to authority of knowledge, as algorithm based digital information is often perceived as faster and more practical than consulting authentic Islamic sources. This study aims to describe how the use of AI affects students' knowledge authority within the framework of the purification of Islamic teachings as articulated by Muhammad Abduh. Employing a phenomenological method, the research involved ten students from various faculties at an Islamic higher education institution. Data were collected through observation, in depth interviews, and documentation, then analyzed through data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion drawing. The findings reveal that while students utilize AI to support academic activities, most of them are not yet able to assess the validity of AI generated information based on the principles of revelation and reason. A phenomenon of "digital taqlid" emerges, in which information is accepted without verification. However, some students demonstrate critical use of AI and balance it with Islamic values, aligning with Abduh's purification framework that emphasizes rationality, ijtihad, and adherence to revelation. This study concludes that AI can be a beneficial tool when used selectively, critically, and grounded in the authoritative epistemology of Islam.

This article examines the multifaceted impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on contemporary English written communication, with particular attention to generative models such as ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs). The analysis centers on written discourse, addressing stylistic formation, textual categories, genre conventions, and the redefinition of linguistic competence within digital contexts. Drawing on discourse analysis, stylistics, and sociolinguistics, the research demonstrates that AI technologies, functioning as both medium and mode of communication, are transforming textual conventions, challenging traditional notions of authorship, and blurring the distinction between human and machine discourse. The central argument asserts that AI operates not only as an autonomous agent in linguistic evolution – generating texts through specific algorithms – but also as a crucial driver of linguistic standardization. This process produces texts lacking human nuance, fosters stylistic and genre hybridization, and contributes to the emergence of a homogenized global form of English. Ultimately, LLMs signify a shift from individual to distributed cognition and from socially determined genre conventions to probabilistic constructions shaped by user input and computational recombination. The study concludes that heightened critical awareness of these developments is vital for preserving linguistic diversity and promoting interpretive literacy in an era increasingly shaped by algorithmic text production.
